chunks: "RISC-V specifies the ISA, not the microarchitecture.
The spec says what instructions exist, what they do, what the registers and privilege modes are, how traps and virtual memory behave and what memory ordering you can rely on.
It says nothing about how many pipeline stages you have, whether you issue in order or out of order, how big the caches are or what branch predictor you use.
Those are design choices for whoever builds the core. That's why you see very different RISC-V cores.
Berkeley's Rocket is a simple in-order pipeline, BOOM is a superscalar out-of-order design, and there are tiny two-stage microcontroller cores and big commercial server-class cores.
They all run the same compliant software, but their area, power and speed are completely different. There are a couple of nuances.
The ISA does constrain the implementation, for example through its weak memory model and precise exceptions, so you can't build anything you like.
And the spec leaves some implementation-defined parameters that software can query, like which extensions are present in the misa register and the vendor and architecture IDs.
But those describe the core; they don't dictate its internals."
